notes.b: Coronary heart disease (CHD) is the narrowing of the coronary arteries, the vessels feeding the heart muscle, by fatty deposits. The aim of the CHD diet is to lower LDL cholesterol and blood pressure and to reduce the strain on the heart and arteries.
points: Replace saturated animal fats with mono- and polyunsaturated oils such as olive, rapeseed and sunflower oil, because saturated fat raises LDL cholesterol, the type that clogs arteries. Use low-cholesterol products where possible.
Choose low-fat dairy products and lean meat, and trim visible fat from meat before cooking. Eat more fish and skinless chicken in place of fatty red meat.
Eat oily fish such as salmon, mackerel and sardines, which supply omega-3 fatty acids.
Increase soluble fibre from oats, beans, lentils, fruit and vegetables, which helps lower LDL cholesterol. Eat more fruit and vegetables in general.
Reduce salt, which helps keep blood pressure down, and use herbs, spices and lemon juice for flavour.
Reduce refined carbohydrate and sugar, such as white bread, sugary foods and sugary drinks, and reduce alcohol.
Use low-fat cooking methods: grill, bake, steam or boil food rather than frying it, avoid creamy sauces, and skim fat from stock and gravy.
A sample day's menu: porridge with low-fat milk and fruit; a wholegrain sandwich with chicken and salad; grilled oily fish with vegetables and potatoes; low-fat yoghurt or fruit.
notes.tip: Exams ask for three or four CHD meal-planning guidelines, or a day's menu with one functional food and the reason for it. Pick distinct guidelines: less saturated fat, unsaturated oils, oily fish, more fibre, less salt, low-fat cooking.

notes.b: Cholesterol is the substance behind the CHD diet. The body needs some of it, but the type and amount in the blood decide whether it helps or harms the arteries.
points: Cholesterol is a soft, wax-like substance found in every body cell, made mainly by the liver and also obtained from animal foods.
Cholesterol forms part of cell membranes and bile, is needed for some hormones, and helps transport fats in the blood.
Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) is associated with saturated fat and deposits cholesterol in artery walls, hardening them. This is why LDL is called the harmful cholesterol.
High-density lipoprotein (HDL) is associated with unsaturated fat and carries cholesterol away from the arteries to the liver.
Lifestyle changes that reduce CHD risk include maintaining a healthy weight, not smoking, avoiding excess alcohol, exercising regularly and reducing stress.
notes.tip: Lifestyle changes are asked alongside diet in CHD questions, so give healthy weight, no smoking, little alcohol, regular exercise and less stress as well as food guidelines.

notes.h: Functional foods for coronary heart disease
notes.b: Some foods are designed to do more than feed you. These functional foods can be added to a CHD menu to help protect the heart.
points: A functional food has health benefits beyond its basic nutritive value, so it does more than supply energy and nutrients.
Plant sterol and stanol spreads, yoghurts, cheese spreads and drinks reduce cholesterol absorption and so lower LDL cholesterol.
Omega-3 enriched eggs and milk supply omega-3 fatty acids.
Prebiotic and probiotic milk and yoghurt improve digestion.
Fortified foods have vitamins and minerals added to them, so they supply nutrients the diet may otherwise lack.
notes.tip: A menu question needs one functional food named with its reason. Plant sterol spreads lowering LDL cholesterol is the safest choice; refer to plant sterol spreads and mycoprotein products rather than brand names.

notes.b: A lacto-vegetarian eats no meat, poultry, fish or eggs, but includes milk and dairy products. Without meat, careful choices are needed to get enough protein, iron, calcium and vitamins.
points: Protein comes from milk, cheese and yoghurt (high biological value protein), and from pulses, nuts, seeds, soya products such as tofu and textured vegetable protein (TVP), and mycoprotein. Combining plant proteins across the day gives a good range of amino acids.
Calcium comes from milk, yoghurt and cheese, and from green leafy vegetables, sesame seeds and fortified soya products. Vitamin D, vitamin C and phosphorus help calcium absorption.
Iron comes from green leafy vegetables, pulses, wholegrains, dried fruit and fortified cereals; vitamin C from fruit and vegetables at the same meal improves absorption.
Vitamin B12 comes from dairy products, vitamin B group from wholegrains, and vitamin D from fortified spreads and cereals and from sunlight. Omega-3 fats come from flaxseed, walnuts and rapeseed oil.
Some cheeses are made with animal rennet, and some mycoprotein products contain egg white, so labels must be checked.
Eggs are excluded, so the diet relies on dairy and pulses for protein and on fortified foods for nutrients that eggs would normally supply.

Other types of vegetarian: lacto-ovo includes eggs and dairy, ovo includes eggs, and pesco includes fish. Some sources also allow eggs in a lacto-vegetarian diet, but the strict definition is dairy yes, eggs no.

People become vegetarian for religious, cultural, moral, health, economic or environmental reasons. A sample day: orange juice, porridge with milk and wholemeal toast; vegetable soup, brown bread, yoghurt and fruit; vegetarian lasagne or a lentil dish with green vegetables.
notes.tip: A lacto-vegetarian does eat dairy, so a statement that the diet includes dairy is true. Do not put eggs in a lacto-vegetarian menu. Exams ask you to define the diet, name two protein alternatives, and give sources of protein, iron or calcium with their helpers, such as vitamin C for iron.

notes.b: A vegan diet excludes all animal-derived foods, including meat, poultry, fish, eggs, milk, cheese and honey. Because dairy and eggs are gone too, a vegan must plan protein, calcium, iron and vitamin B12 from plant and fortified sources.
points: Protein comes from pulses, nuts, seeds, soya products, vegan mycoprotein, seitan and tempeh; eating pulses with grains or nuts over the day provides all the essential amino acids.
Vitamin B12 has no reliable plant source, so it must come from fortified foods such as soya milk, cereals and yeast extract, or from a supplement.
Calcium comes from fortified soya milk and flour, calcium-set tofu, sesame seeds in tahini, nuts, vegan cheese, and broccoli, spinach and other dark green vegetables.
Iron comes from pulses, wholegrains, dried fruit, dark green vegetables and fortified cereals; vitamin C from peppers, tomatoes, berries and citrus improves absorption.
Vitamin D comes from fortified foods and sunlight, and omega-3 fats from flaxseed, walnuts and rapeseed oil.

Hidden animal ingredients can turn up in stock cubes, some spreads, some bread and sweets (gelatine) and in cheese made with rennet, so choose labelled vegan products and check for gelatine, milk powder, egg, rennet or honey.
A vegan menu example uses vegan mycoprotein mince, lentils or beans, vegetables and fruit, which excludes animal products and still supplies protein, iron, calcium and fortified B12.
notes.tip: Vegan questions ask for sources of protein, calcium and iron, or a vegan menu with an explanation of how it meets vegan needs. Always include a B12 source, because vegetarians get B12 from dairy but vegans cannot.

notes.b: Coeliac disease is a lifelong intolerance to gluten, the protein found in wheat, barley and rye. The only treatment is a strict gluten-free diet.
points: Gluten damages the villi, the finger-like lining of the small intestine, so food is not properly absorbed and deficiencies of iron, calcium and folate can develop.

Avoid bread, cakes, biscuits, pastries, pizzas and pies made with wheat, ordinary pasta and couscous, seitan, and processed foods such as sausages, some soups, sauces and gravies. Wheat, barley, rye and malt are all sources of gluten.

Build meals around naturally gluten-free staples such as rice, corn (maize), potatoes, buckwheat, soya products and lentils, plus meat, fish, eggs, dairy, fruit and vegetables. Gluten-free versions of bread, pasta and flour are also available.
Check ingredient lists for hidden gluten in stock, sauces, malt products and processed meats, and look for the gluten-free symbol or declaration on products.
A gluten-free claim means the food as sold contains no more than 20 mg of gluten per kilogram (Regulation (EU) No 828/2014, FSAI guidance). Wheat and oats used must still appear in the ingredients.

Avoid cross-contamination in the kitchen, for example by using a separate toaster and utensils, so crumbs of gluten do not reach safe food. Oats are naturally gluten-free but often contaminated, so use only oats labelled gluten-free.
Gluten-free breads and cereals are often low in fibre, so choose brown rice, beans and other high-fibre gluten-free foods.
Replace the iron, calcium and folate normally supplied by wheat products with other naturally gluten-free or fortified sources.
notes.tip: Coeliac questions ask you to define the condition, name three foods to avoid and give three meal-planning guidelines. Remember that seitan and ordinary couscous contain gluten, and vegan meat products may too, so vegan and coeliac are different diets.

notes.b: The diabetic diet aims to keep blood glucose stable, maintain a healthy weight and reduce the risk of heart disease. It does not mean no carbohydrate; it means carbohydrate that is low-GI, regular and controlled.
points: Regular meals and snacks at set times prevent large swings in blood glucose; skipping meals is avoided.
Low-glycaemic-index (GI) carbohydrates such as wholegrain bread, oats, pasta and pulses release glucose slowly, so blood glucose rises gradually. High-fibre foods and plenty of vegetables also help.
Refined sugar, sugar-sweetened soft drinks, sweets and sugar-laden processed foods are avoided or limited, and low-calorie sweeteners can replace sugar.
Fibre-rich fruit and vegetables and low-sugar fruits are chosen, as high-sugar fruit should be limited.
Saturated fat and salt are reduced, and unsaturated oils are used instead, because diabetes raises the risk of heart disease. Keeping a healthy weight and exercising also help.
Insulin dose is matched to the carbohydrate eaten in people using insulin, so meal timing and portions must be consistent.
notes.tip: Diabetes questions ask for three dietary guidelines: eliminate refined sugar, eat regular meals, choose low-GI carbohydrate or more fibre. Do not write that a diabetic avoids all carbohydrate.

notes.h: How manufacturers and retailers meet special dietary needs
notes.b: People on modified diets need suitable foods that are easy to find and easy to use. Manufacturers and retailers both respond to this.
points: Manufacturers produce specialised ranges such as gluten-free, diabetic, vegetarian and coronary heart disease products.
Manufacturers give detailed labels and packet recipes, and offer smaller portion sizes for people who need them.
Retailers provide specialist shops or sections, designated shelves and wider ranges of special-diet foods, so customers can find suitable products quickly.
Retailers run in-store cookery demonstrations to show customers how to use special-diet products, and provide information and websites.
notes.tip: Examiners ask you to describe measures taken by manufacturers and retailers for consumers with specific dietary requirements, so give separate points for each group.

notes.b: Labels let people on special diets check quickly whether a food is suitable. What the label shows, and how far it can be trusted, is what exams focus on.
points: The name of the food and ingredients must be listed in descending order of weight, so the main ingredients are easy to identify.
Under Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, given effect in Ireland by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014, allergens must be highlighted in the ingredient list.
Nutrition information shows the energy, fat, saturated fat, sugar, salt and fibre content of the food.
Symbols and claims show gluten-free, vegetarian and vegan status and whether a food is fortified, functional, low-fat or reduced-sugar, which helps people with specific needs choose.
Labels give cooking and storage instructions, the net quantity, the use-by or best-before date, the origin and any GM ingredients, helping people choose foods safely.
Labels are useful but must be read critically: claims can mislead, small print can hide gluten, and 'may contain' warnings need checking.
notes.tip: Labelling questions ask you to explain or evaluate labels for people with specific needs, so give what labels show and then a limitation, such as misleading claims or hidden gluten.

keyTerms.definition: A person who eats no meat, poultry, fish or eggs, but includes milk and dairy products in the diet.
A diet that excludes all animal-derived foods, including meat, fish, eggs, dairy products and honey.
A lifelong intolerance to gluten that damages the villi of the small intestine and reduces the absorption of nutrients.
A protein found in wheat, barley and rye that causes damage to the small intestine in people with coeliac disease.
Compounds found naturally in plants that reduce the absorption of cholesterol from the gut when added to foods.
A ranking of carbohydrate foods by how quickly they raise blood glucose; low-GI foods release glucose slowly.
A food that provides health benefits beyond its basic nutritive value, such as plant sterol spreads or probiotic yoghurt.
Low-density lipoprotein, the form of cholesterol that carries cholesterol to artery walls and is linked with saturated fat.
High-density lipoprotein, the form of cholesterol that carries cholesterol away from the arteries and is linked with unsaturated fat.
A protein food made from a fungus, used in mycoprotein products; vegan versions contain no egg.

questions.prompt: Outline three meal planning guidelines for a person following a lacto-vegetarian diet.
questions.model: Include protein at every meal from milk, cheese, yoghurt, pulses, nuts, seeds and soya products. Include calcium-rich dairy such as milk, yoghurt and cheese each day. Pair iron-rich foods such as pulses, wholegrains and green leafy vegetables with a source of vitamin C at the same meal. Also check labels for egg in mycoprotein products and for animal rennet in cheese. Any three guidelines, each explained, earn 6 marks.

questions.prompt: Discuss the dietary guidelines to follow when planning and preparing meals for a person with coronary heart disease, including the role of functional foods.
questions.model: Reduce saturated fat by replacing animal fats with mono- and polyunsaturated oils, choosing lean meat, fish and low-fat dairy, and trimming visible fat. Eat oily fish for omega-3 fatty acids. Increase soluble fibre from oats, beans, lentils, fruit and vegetables to lower LDL cholesterol. Reduce salt and refined carbohydrate and sugar. Use cooking methods such as grilling, baking, steaming or boiling, and avoid creamy sauces. Functional foods: plant sterol and stanol spreads reduce cholesterol absorption; omega-3 eggs and milk reduce heart-disease risk; prebiotic and probiotic dairy improves digestion. Lifestyle: maintain a healthy weight, do not smoke, limit alcohol and exercise regularly.
